# Captions, image and sound

## Captions

Caption the words that remain audible in the final cut. Verify uncertain terms against the audio, especially Czech diacritics, names, numbers, technical terms and clipped first or last words. On the Remotion path, transcribe the full source for selection, then align the chosen words to the assembled audio for final timing. The FFmpeg path already does this. Inspect active-word changes at the first and last word of each cut; neither should flash early or persist into the next phrase.

Use short semantic groups, usually 2–5 words, with line breaks at natural phrase boundaries. Keep punctuation and case readable. For an ordinary footage-led Reel, default to white captions with a restrained shadow or outline directly over the picture; use a backing only when needed for contrast. Use one accent color and highlight the active or meaning-bearing word, not every word at once. Bold or energetic type is appropriate when performance and brand call for it; animation should settle quickly enough to read. Avoid the look of a news bulletin: no default headline banner, permanent lower third, ticker, stacked information boxes or graphic frame. Avoid visual noise from a permanent progress bar, repeated flashes or constantly rotating colors.

Inspect the longest caption and high-motion shots at phone size. Keep text away from faces, important UI and platform controls. Safe areas differ by app, placement and description length, so use current platform previews or a conservative lower-middle position and verify it visually. If source captions are burned in, crop, cover deliberately or use a clean source; do not allow two conflicting caption layers.

## Image

Inspect the start, middle and end of every chosen segment and more often when a subject moves. Stabilize framing before adding motion. Put faces where eyes read naturally, but keep the hands or product when they carry the claim. For landscape screens, an aggressive 9:16 crop may destroy the information; use a designed card, readable inset or staged zoom that follows the narration. Track a face or cursor only when the detected motion is reliable and the resulting crop does not jitter.

Use B-roll to show a named object, step, location, result or proof. Time its appearance to the relevant spoken words. A simple jump cut or gentle punch can support emphasis; default to no transition between ordinary speech cuts. Tighten edits around complete thoughts and visible action when the source supports a brisk pace. Do not mask a weak narrative with effects, automatic camera drift or a graphic on every cut.

## Sound

Mix speech first. Preserve intelligibility on a phone speaker and avoid chopped breaths, clicks and ambience jumps at seams. Add music only if it establishes tone without masking consonants; reduce it under speech and fade it cleanly at the ending. For a music-led motion section, align major reveals and match cuts to audible accents. Add a quiet click, pop or whoosh only on an actual cut, action or semantic beat that benefits from it. Do not scatter effects at fixed intervals. Listen to the finished mix for pumping, harsh sibilance, clipping and a truncated final syllable. Loudness targets are a finishing guide, not a substitute for listening.
